source: Lassiter & Goodman (2012) How many kinds of reasoning? Inference, probability, and natural language semantics (CogSci 34)
finding: Full text read this session, so the earlier 'could not re-verify' gap is closed. They put the modal word inside the conclusion, so the same people judged 'necessary' and 'plausible' on the same kind of argument. The sensitivity gap seen between groups in Heit-Rotello showed up within one person. Their model treats each modal word as a nonlinear function of one probability scale.
numbers: 507 recruited on Mechanical Turk, 485 native-English analysed, 10,185 judgments. Each person saw 21 two-premise arguments drawn from 63 (36 invalid, 27 valid). Necessary: valid .82, invalid .41, d' 1.15 +/- .19. Plausible: valid .94, invalid .82, d' 0.63 +/- .27. Difference in d' significant at p<.05. Six modals plus a no-modal control (possible, plausible, likely, probable, necessary, certain).
quote: the difference previously reported can be elicited by a difference of a single modal word
limits: Correction to K03: N analysed is 485 (507 recruited). Natural biological predicates (enzymes, bones) pushed invalid acceptance far above novel-property stimuli, which lowered d' in both conditions. Authors did not find the Rips crossover (footnote). Conference paper, not a journal article. Only binary agree/disagree is analysed; a 5-point confidence rating was collected.
agent_relevance: A one-word change inside one judge moves d'. So a d' gap between 'necessary' and 'plausible' wording is expected even with one strength scale. An agent test must look at rank order, not at d' alone.

source: Lassiter & Goodman (2012) model fit and rank-order test
finding: Test of whether 'necessary' and 'plausible' answers share a rank order (gap 8). The model says the order of arguments by acceptance must be the same in every modal frame, only bent by a power law. Observed order agreement was moderate, not perfect, and about what noise alone would give.
numbers: Mean Spearman rank correlation across all pairs of modal frames .53 (permutation p<.0001). Simulated data from the best-fit model, whose true rank correlation is 1: 95% of simulated values .49 to .64, mean .57. Model R2 by modal: certain .60, likely .55, necessary .57, plausible .42, possible .32, probable .41. Mean split-half R2: .66, .57, .70, .37, .34, .47. Best-fit noise parameter .12.
quote: This does not rule out a qualitative distinction between inductive and deductive reasoning
limits: Fit uses a free exponent per modal, so the test is soft. Necessary R2 .57 is below its split-half ceiling .70, so some real structure is unexplained. Plausible R2 .42 is above its split-half .37. Short two-premise animal-property arguments only. Authors say the result 'does not rule out a qualitative distinction'.
agent_relevance: Supports a single-scale design for the agent, but only weakly. The agent can run its own version: same items, two wordings, compare rank order against a noise ceiling from repeated samples.

source: Hayes, Stephens, Ngo & Dunn (2018) The dimensionality of reasoning (re-read for state-trace method, base-rate and speed results)
finding: Re-read for gaps 2 and 4. A state-trace plot puts mean accept rate under induction wording against mean accept rate under deduction wording across conditions. If the points rise monotonically, one latent dimension is enough. Stephens et al. (2017) applied it to 26 earlier studies and found the data fit one strength dimension with two independent criteria. A new experiment in that work moved the two criteria in opposite directions by beliefs about base rates of plausible versus valid items. In Experiment 3 here, speeding shifted endorsement in opposite directions for induction and deduction, yet one dimension still fit.
numbers: Three experiments, N=122, 110, 122, all causal conditional arguments (valid/invalid x believable/unbelievable), 16 target items. Combined analyses had 24 conditions per state-trace plot.
limits: Base-rate experiment numbers belong to Stephens, Dunn & Hayes (2018, Psych Review), which is paywalled and was not opened; here it is second-hand. Monotone plots are a weak test (see Ashby critique, b12).
agent_relevance: Two cutoffs on one scale can be moved separately by framing, speed and stated base rates. Good news for a stakes-driven threshold in the agent, but the human proof covers causal conditionals only.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM: accuracy table and where the solver loses
finding: Full text read. GPT-4 with chain of thought beats the solver pipeline only on PrOntoQA. On the four other sets the solver wins. The loss comes from the translation step failing, and that step fails more on real expert-written problems than on synthetic ones.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy, CoT vs Logic-LM (no refinement): PrOntoQA 98.79 vs 83.20; ProofWriter 68.11 vs 79.66; FOLIO 70.58 vs 78.92; LogicalDeduction 75.25 vs 87.63; AR-LSAT 35.06 vs 43.04. GPT-4 executable-formula rate: PrOntoQA 100%, ProofWriter 99.0%, LogicalDeduction 100%, FOLIO 79.9%, AR-LSAT 32.6%. Self-refinement raised executable rate by 5.01 points on average. Authors: CoT forward chaining fits PrOntoQA and ProofWriter; solvers suit hypothesising, conditioning, elimination.
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5, text-davinci-003, GPT-4). When a formula did not run, the pipeline fell back to CoT, so Logic-LM numbers mix both. PrOntoQA subset: 5-hop fictional names, 500 items. No token-matched comparison.
agent_relevance: Crossover rule of thumb: short forward-chain synthetic problems, or any case where translation is hard, stay with the model. Deep, non-linear or constraint-style problems with clean statements go to the solver, with a fallback when the formula does not run.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: effect of reasoning depth
finding: On ProofWriter the solver's edge over CoT grows with proof depth, because the translation job does not get harder when the proof does.
numbers: Logic-LM minus CoT by depth (0, <=1, <=2, <=4, <=5 hops; 300 items per subset, as the text lists them): +7.1, +5.0, +12.7, +20.0, +39.4 points.
limits: The paragraph does not name the base model next to these numbers; the figure shows several models. Depth is synthetic.
agent_relevance: Use proof depth (number of chained steps) as a routing signal: shallow goes to the model, deep goes to a solver or code.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation
finding: Same pattern as Logic-LM from an independent team, with a failure analysis. On FOLIO GPT-4 with CoT and with the solver tie. On ProofWriter the solver wins big. The solver is the more conservative judge: it says 'Uncertain' much more often.
numbers: FOLIO GPT-4 average accuracy CoT 75.3% vs LINC 72.5%; McNemar p=0.58. ProofWriter (balanced subset): LINC with GPT-3.5 96.4%, with GPT-4 98.3%; StarCoder+ with LINC beats GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 CoT by 38 and 10 points. Mean premises per question 5.3 (FOLIO) vs 18.8 (ProofWriter). Predicted labels on FOLIO, GPT-4: CoT 32% True, 27% False, 41% Uncertain; LINC 24% / 17% / 57%, 2% errors. FOL syntax errors: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4.
limits: 2023 models. Failure modes differ: LINC loses implicit facts and merges predicates; CoT commits the fallacy of the converse and misses long paths. The agreement counts in the confusion figure were garbled in extraction and are not quoted.
agent_relevance: Two checkers with different errors can run together; disagreement flags the items worth a look. The solver acts as a high-criterion validity check (lower recall, higher precision).

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-aided language models using declarative prompting
finding: A solver-based approach also beats CoT on deep logic and constraint problems, and it can abstain when the formula is unsatisfiable or ambiguous.
numbers: code-davinci-002, greedy decoding: ProofWriter depth-5 CoT 80.1 vs SatLM 99.7; LSAT 23.5 vs 35.0; BoardgameQA 60.7 vs 79.4; CLUTRR 40.8 vs 68.3. GSM word problems: SatLM 71.8 vs program-aided 72.7 (on par). Replacing the solver with a CoT solver lowered accuracy; removing it entirely gave about standard-prompting accuracy. Selective accuracy rises because SatLM answers fewer items (UNSAT and AMBIG abstain).
limits: Older code model; no modern reasoning model. Abstention raises selective accuracy but lowers coverage.
agent_relevance: A solver gives a third outcome besides valid and invalid: cannot decide. The agent should keep that outcome and not force yes or no.

source: Thatikonda, Han, Buntine, Shareghi (2026) Improving Symbolic Translation of Language Models for Logical Reasoning
finding: Abstract and introduction read. Small models are the weak point of translate-then-solve: format and predicate errors, and self-repair from solver error messages depends on model size. Splitting translation into two stages (predicates first, then formulas) plus a predicate-arity verifier reduced errors.
numbers: Three model families, four logical-reasoning datasets, an error taxonomy for syntax errors. No headline accuracy figure extracted.
limits: Intro only; tables not checked. Targets small open models, not the agent's model.
agent_relevance: The check route needs a translation guard: two-stage translation and arity verification before trusting a solver's 'invalid'.

source: Poddar, Sahoo, Ghosh (2025) Understanding Syllogistic Reasoning in LLMs from Formal and Natural Language Perspectives (full text, CoT and criterion)
finding: Gaps 7 and 1. Zero-shot chain of thought gave no change from plain zero-shot across 14 models, but the CoT cue was only 'think step by step' and the answer was one word. Models differ a lot in how liberal or strict they are about saying 'valid', which is a criterion difference. From the reported precision and recall plus the item base rate, a strict model and a lenient model can be roughly compared on d'.
numbers: 160 syllogisms (76 valid, 84 invalid). 14 models x 3 temperatures x 4 prompting strategies. ZS vs ZS-CoT McNemar chi2=1, p=.612 (389 vs 374 discordant, N=6,720 per comparison). Few-shot below zero-shot by 3.57 points (p_adj=.0495). Qwen3-Next 80B Thinking: precision 99.2%, recall 42.8%. Gemma 3 27B: recall 93.1%, precision 61.0%. My derived estimate from these and the 47.5% valid base rate: Qwen d' about 2.55, c about +1.46 (very strict); Gemma d' about 1.39, c about -0.79 (lenient).
limits: The derived d' and c are my arithmetic, not the paper's; precision and recall may be pooled over strategies and temperatures. Models are mostly open or small. No equal-token control for CoT. Authors chose accuracy gaps over ROC.
agent_relevance: Criterion varies by model and prompt more than sensitivity does. The agent should measure its own cutoff and not assume one. CoT being null here conflicts with Bertolazzi, so equal-token CoT stays open.

source: Poddar et al. (2025) belief bias and dual ground truth
finding: With two labels per item (does it follow, is it believable) models that are good at form are near chance on believability, and weak models lean on believability. This is the direct picture of two questions with two different answers.
numbers: Mean syntax accuracy 81.7%, believability accuracy 56.2%. Gemini 2.5 Flash 99.6% syntax with a 47.9 point syntax-minus-believability gap; GPT-OSS-20B gap 47.9; Gemini 2.5 Pro 47.4; Llama 3.2 3B gap -14.5; Llama 3.2 1B -8.5. Belief bias (congruent minus incongruent accuracy) mean +10.81 points, 12 of 14 models positive, t13=2.47, p=.028, d=0.66; top models under 2 points, worst +46.9. Spearman of syntax accuracy with bias -0.565 (p=.035).
limits: Only 38 of 160 items (23.8%) have believable conclusions. The accuracy-gap measure is the kind of index Heit and Rotello criticise.
agent_relevance: Strong models can answer the validity question without leaking belief; weak ones cannot. Per-item wording choice matters most for weak or small sub-models.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks (re-read for interaction and answer bias)
finding: LLMs repeat the human interaction: belief-consistent conclusions get 'valid' whatever the logic, while for belief-violating conclusions models are more sensitive to real validity. That is a belief-by-validity interaction under one wording. Raw answer likelihoods show a large yes-bias in some models.
numbers: Significant belief x validity interaction in humans, PaLM 2-L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5 (all z>5.9, p<.001). With raw-likelihood scoring several models answered 'valid' to every syllogism; removing the instruction prompt reduced that bias and showed stronger content effects. 5-shot Chinchilla: content effects slightly weaker on syllogisms, exaggerated on Wason.
limits: One wording only ('valid'); no plausible-wording arm. The likelihood correction (DC-PMI) is itself a criterion correction.
agent_relevance: Any wording test in the agent must first measure and subtract a global yes-bias, or a criterion shift will look like a sensitivity change.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt, Bernardi (2024) A Systematic Analysis of LLMs as Soft Reasoners: The Case of Syllogistic Inferences
finding: Gap 10 and gap 1 side evidence. Zero-shot CoT in LLaMA-3 is lenient on invalid syllogisms (almost never says 'nothing follows'); instruction tuning partly fixes this. Accuracy falls as the premise chain grows, and only supervised fine-tuning holds up.
numbers: LLaMA-3 8B ZS-CoT accuracy on unseen premise counts: 2 premises 44.64, 3 premises 39.64, 4 premises 31.79. Pythia 1.4B ZS-CoT 18.21, 11.07, 7.86. SFT LLaMA-3 8B 99.05, 94.17, 85.36. Humans (Khemlani & Johnson-Laird) 44.63% on valid and 40.97% on invalid schemas. LLaMA models match or beat humans on valid schemas but cannot recognise invalid ones; instruction tuning helps invalid and costs valid.
limits: Open small models, a generation task (produce a conclusion), not a yes/no accept task. Not the Heit-Rotello design.
agent_relevance: Longer premise chains cost accuracy even on fixed forms, so premise count should trigger decomposition or a solver step.

source: Han, Ransom, Perfors, Kemp (2024) Inductive reasoning in humans and large language models (re-read)
finding: Gap 10. GPT-4 matches humans on most of 11 property-induction phenomena but fails premise non-monotonicity, going the wrong way on specific arguments, and its stated reasoning is 'more examples make it stronger'. GPT-3.5 matched humans better than GPT-4 on general arguments; the authors link this to RLHF.
numbers: gpt-4-0314 at temperature 0, 400-token cap; GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003) scored from token probabilities. Experiment 1: 11 phenomena x 3 domains. Non-monotonicity: GPT-3.5 leans the wrong way on General arguments; GPT-4 strongly wrong on Specific ones. Experiment 2: for single-premise General Mammals arguments GPT-4 is uncorrelated with human ratings.
limits: 2023 models. Premise count and odd premises were not swept with the agent's current model.
agent_relevance: Treat an extra odd premise as a possible weakener and ask for it by name; do not let the agent read added premises as added strength.

source: Cacioli (2026) LLMs as Signal Detectors: Sensitivity, Bias, and the Temperature-Criterion Analogy
finding: First full signal-detection treatment of LLMs found. LLM criterion knobs are not clean: raising temperature changed both criterion and sensitivity, because it changes the generated answer. Instruct models show strongly unequal-variance evidence, which breaks equal-variance d'.
numbers: Pre-registered; 168,000 confidence-rating trials plus 6,000 forced-choice trials; Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Llama-3-8B-Base; seven temperatures; factual QA. Temperature raised AUC by 0.071 to 0.146 while shifting criterion. z-ROC slopes 0.52-0.84 (instruct 0.52-0.63, base 0.77-0.87, human recognition memory about 0.80).
limits: Factual question answering, not reasoning; small open models. Wording was not tested.
agent_relevance: Use unequal-variance d_a or AUC and not plain d' in any agent test, and use prompt wording as the criterion lever, not temperature.

source: Abe et al. (2026) Abductive Reasoning with Syllogistic Forms in Large Language Models
finding: Closest thing found to a task-framing contrast in LLMs: the same syllogistic forms asked as 'which hypothesis is the most plausible explanation' (abduction) and as 'does it follow' (deduction). Items are converted, not identical, so this is not the Rips design. LLMs are poor at saying 'neither', and belief-inconsistent items cost accuracy in both.
numbers: 216 items per task. GPT-4 zero-shot deduction: overall 72.22%, 'Neither' 44.44%, consistent 74.24%, inconsistent 68.18%. GPT-4 few-shot deduction 95.83% (Neither 94.44%). GPT-4 zero-shot abduction about 42%. GPT-3.5 few-shot deduction 46.30%, Neither 2.78%. Llama-3-70B few-shot deduction 84.72% vs abduction 75.46%.
limits: Different items for the two framings; small and older models; accuracy only.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples that include a 'nothing follows' case may shift the agent's validity criterion a lot; a cheap test.

source: Chan, Gaizauskas, Zhao (2026) Position: Logical soundness is not a reliable criterion for neurosymbolic fact-checking with LLMs (ICLR 2026 workshop)
finding: Position paper; introduction and framing read. It argues that a valid conclusion from true premises can still mislead readers, and that LLMs' human-like inference habits can be used to flag such cases. No new experiment in the part read.
numbers: No experiments reported in the sections read.
limits: Opinion, not evidence. A pointer only to the 'validity is not enough' side of the plausibility-versus-validity choice.
agent_relevance: When the output goes to a reader, run both checks: validity of the step, then what the reader would infer from it.

source: Stephens, Dunn, Hayes (2018) Are there two processes in reasoning? Psychological Review 125(2), 218-244 (abstract level only)
finding: Seen only as a repository abstract in a search result: almost all testable models were rejected, including all two-dimensional models; the one model that fit all three data sets had one strength dimension with independent decision criteria for induction and deduction. The base-rate experiment is described by Hayes et al. (see d03).
numbers: Abstract-level only; no N or fit statistics.
limits: Not opened (paywalled). Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Same as d03. A base-rate or stakes lever on the two cutoffs has human support here, not LLM support.

source: Search record: LLM versions of Rips, Heit-Rotello, or state-trace designs (gaps 1, 2, 4)
finding: Searches this session (web search and arXiv listing) for an LLM run through 'necessary' versus 'plausible' wording with ROC or d', or a state-trace plot for an LLM, found none. The nearest are d09, d11, d14 and d15. Web search quota ran out partway through, so this is a limited negative search.
numbers: No study found for gaps 1, 2, 3 (token-matched), 4 (base-rate or stakes manipulations), 5 (new) or 7 (closed models at equal tokens).
limits: Absence from a limited search, not proof of absence. The query on Heit-Rotello generalisation (gap 5) hit the quota, so gap 5 rests on earlier evidence only.
agent_relevance: These gaps need a small experiment on the agent itself. The design is in the critique addendum.
